title: If all things recur, nothing is in our power
source_text: Οὐκ οἶδα δὲ πῶς χρήσιμον ἔδοξε τῷ Κέλσῳ καθ᾿ ἡμῶν γράφοντι παραῤῥίψαι δόγμα, πολλῆς δεόμενον κἂν δοκούσης ἀποδείξεως, κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν παριστάσης ὅτι ὁμοία ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς εἰς τέλος ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν θνητῶν περίοδος, καὶ κατὰ τὰς τεταγμένας ἀνακυκλήσεις ἀνάγκη τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεὶ καὶ γεγονέναι καὶ εἶναι καὶ ἔσεσθαι. ὅπερ ἐὰν ᾖ ἀληθὲς. τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀνῄρηται. εἰ γὰρ κατὰ (τὰς) τεταγμένας ἀνακυκλήσεις ἀνάγκη τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεὶ καὶ γεγονέναι καὶ εἶναι καὶ ἔσεσθαι ἐν τῇ τῶν θνητῶν περιόδῳ. δῆλον ὅτι ἀνάγκη ἀεὶ Σωκράτη μὲν φιλοσοφήσειν καὶ κατηγορηθήσεσθαι ἐπὶ καινοῖς δαιμονίοις καὶ τῇ τῶν νέων διαφθορᾷ, Ἄνυτον δὲ καὶ Μέλητον ἀεὶ κατηγορήσειν αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὴν ἐν Ἀρείῳ πάγῳ βουλὴν καταψηφίσεσθαι αὐτοῦ τὸν διὰ τοῦ κωνείου θάνατον. οὕτω δὲ ἀνάγκη ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰς τεταγμένας περιόδους Φάλαριν τυραννήσειν καὶ τὸν Φεραῖον Ἀλέξανδρον τὰ αὐτὰ ὠμοποιήσειν, τούς τε εἰς τὸν Φαλάριδος ταῦρον καταδικασθέντας ἀεὶ ἐν αὐτῷ μυκήσεσθαι· ἅπερ ἐὰν δοθῇ. οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν σωθήσεται καὶ ἔπαινοι καὶ ψόγοι εὐλόγως ἔσονται. λελέξεται δὲ πρὸς τὴν τοιαύτην ὑπόθεσιν τῷ Κέλσῳ ὅτι. εἴπερ ὁμοία ἐστὶν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς εἰς τέλος ἡ τῶν θνητῶν ἀεὶ περίοδος. καὶ κατὰ τὰς τεταγμένας ἀνακυκλήσεις ἀνάγκη τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεὶ καὶ γεγονέναι καὶ εἶναι καὶ ἔσεσθαι, ἀνάγκη ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰς τεταγμένας περιόδους Μωϋσέα μὲν μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐξελθεῖν ἐκ τῆς Αἰγύπτου. Ἰησοῦν δὲ πάλιν ἐπιδημῆσαι τῷ βίῳ τὰ αὐτὰ ποιήσοντα, ἅπερ οὐχ ἅπαξ ἀλλ᾿ ἀπειράκις κατὰ περιόδους πεποίηκεν· ἀλλὰ καὶ Χριστιανοὶ οἱ αὐτοὶ ἔσονται ἐν ταῖς τεταγμέναις ἀνακυκλήσεσιν, καὶ πάλιν Κέλσος γράψει τὸ βιβλίον τοῦτο. ἀπειράκις αὐτὸ πρότερον γράψας.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know (οἶδα) how it seemed useful (χρήσιμον, δοκέω) to Celsus writing against us to throw in by the way (παραρρίπτω) a doctrine (δόγμα) needing much demonstration (ἀπόδειξις), even a seeming one, establishing (παρίστημι) as far as possible that [Celsus:] alike (ὅμοιος) from beginning (ἀρχή) to end (τέλος) is the cycle (περίοδος) of mortals (θνητοί), and according to the appointed (τάσσω) revolutions (ἀνακύκλησις) it is necessary (ἀνάγκη) that the same things always (ἀεί) have come to be and be and be going to be. Which if it is true, what is in our power (τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν) is taken away (ἀναιρέω). For if according to the appointed revolutions the same things must always have been, be and will be in the cycle of mortals, clearly it is necessary that Socrates always will philosophize (φιλοσοφέω) and be accused (κατηγορέω) on new divinities (καινὰ δαιμόνια) and the corruption (διαφθορά) of the young, and Anytus and Meletus always will accuse him, and the council (βουλή) on the Areopagus (Ἄρειος πάγος) will vote against (καταψηφίζομαι) him death by hemlock (κώνειον). So too it is necessary always according to the appointed cycles that Phalaris will be tyrant (τυραννέω) and Alexander of Pherae will commit the same cruelties (ὠμοποιέω), and those condemned (καταδικάζω) into Phalaris’s bull (ταῦρος) always will bellow (μυκάομαι) in it; which if granted (δίδωμι), I do not know how what is in our power will be saved (σῴζω) and praises (ἔπαινοι) and blames (ψόγοι) will be reasonable (εὐλόγως). It will be said to Celsus against such a hypothesis (ὑπόθεσις) that, if alike from beginning to end is always the cycle of mortals, and according to the appointed revolutions the same things must always have been, be and will be, it is necessary always according to the appointed cycles that Moses with the people of the Jews go out (ἐξέρχομαι) from Egypt, and Jesus again sojourn (ἐπιδημέω) in life (βίος) to do the same things, which not once (ἅπαξ) but countless times (ἀπειράκις) by cycles he has done; but also the same Christians will be in the appointed revolutions, and again Celsus will write this book (βιβλίον), having written it countless times before.
pass_b_english: I do not know how Celsus, writing against us, thought it useful to toss in a doctrine that needs a great deal of proof, even if only plausible proof, to establish as far as possible that “the cycle of mortal things is alike from beginning to end, and according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be.” If this is true, what lies in our power is abolished.

For if “according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be” in the cycle of mortal things, then clearly Socrates must always practise philosophy and always be accused on the charge of new divinities and of corrupting the young; Anytus and Meletus must always accuse him; and the council on the Areopagus must always vote to condemn him to death by hemlock. In the same way, according to the appointed cycles, Phalaris must always rule as a tyrant, Alexander of Pherae must always commit the same cruelties, and those condemned to Phalaris’s bull must always bellow inside it. If this is granted, I do not know how what lies in our power will be kept safe, or how praise and blame will be reasonable.

Against such a hypothesis this will be said to Celsus: if the cycle of mortal things is always alike from beginning to end, and according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be, then according to the appointed cycles Moses must always go out of Egypt with the people of the Jews, and Jesus must come again to dwell in this life to do the same things that he has done, not once but countless times, cycle after cycle. Indeed, the same Christians too will exist in the appointed revolutions, and Celsus will write this book again, having written it countless times before.

choices.choice: Celsus's formula 'must always have been, and be, and be going to be' (stiff) made 'it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be', used the same way all three times
'needs a great deal of proof, even proof that is merely plausible, to show as far as it can' made 'even if only plausible proof, to establish as far as possible' (participle agrees with the proof)
'always be a philosopher' made 'always practise philosophy' (φιλοσοφήσειν is a verb)
'accused of bringing in new divinities' made 'accused on the charge of new divinities' ('bringing in' is not in the Greek)
'be a tyrant' made 'rule as a tyrant' (τυραννήσειν)

Celsus’s words (from his ‘True Doctrine’) are in double quotation marks; Origen repeats the formula later in the chapter in his own counter-argument without a quotation frame, so it is left unquoted there. Text: Koetschau prints “κατὰ (τὰς) τεταγμένας” with the article supplied; translated as supplied. ‘τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν’ rendered “what lies in our power” (the free-choice term) rather than ‘free will’. ‘πολλῆς δεόμενον κἂν δοκούσης ἀποδείξεως’ taken as ‘needing much proof, even if only a plausible one’. Origen names the Areopagus council as Socrates’ judges; historically the trial was before a popular court, but the Greek is translated as it stands. The charges echo the indictment reported in Plato, Apology 24b, but Origen does not quote it, so no inline source is given. Moses’ going out of Egypt refers to the Exodus narrative as an event, not to a quoted verse, so no inline citation is given. ‘ἐπιδημῆσαι τῷ βίῳ’ = ‘come to dwell in this life’ (Origen’s usual word for Christ’s coming among men).
